questions.question: What three topics does chapter 14 say it covers?
questions.answer: An introduction to NLP, preprocessing text input into numeric input, and building simple text classification models.
questions.explanation: These are the three bullets of the 'This chapter covers' box.

questions.question: According to the page, what distinguishes machine languages like LISP from natural languages?
options: Machine languages were designed: their formal rules came before their use
Natural languages have no rules at all
questions.answer: Machine languages were designed: their formal rules came before their use
questions.explanation: The page says every machine language began with an engineer writing formal rules, and use came after. Vocabulary size isn't mentioned. Machine languages do define meaning. Natural languages do have rules, but they were formalised after the fact (p.406).

questions.question: Why does it matter for NLP that natural language's rules came after its usage?
questions.answer: Because its rules weren't designed upfront, they are incomplete, full of exceptions and constantly changing, so hand-writing a complete rule set is impractical. That motivates learning patterns from data.
questions.explanation: The page sets up this contrast, and p.406 draws the conclusion: natural language is messy, and rule-based systems struggled to generalise.

questions.question: Looking at the chapter outline, can you explain the difference between a 'set model' and a 'sequence model' before reading section 14.3?
questions.answer: Hypothesis to check later: a set model treats a text as an unordered collection of tokens (bag-of-words), while a sequence model processes tokens in order (e.g. an RNN).
questions.explanation: Predicting from the outline primes you for the chapter's central comparison (p.419).

questions.question: Which model does the page say this chapter sets the stage for, and in which chapter does it appear?
questions.answer: The Transformer, in the next chapter (chapter 15, 'Language models and the Transformer').
questions.explanation: The introductory paragraph mentions building more complicated models, like the Transformer, in the next chapter.

questions.question: What did the early-1950s IBM-Georgetown translation system consist of?
options: A neural network trained on parallel corpora
Six hardcoded grammar rules and a lookup table of a couple of hundred words and suffixes
A decision tree learned from Russian newspapers
A statistical model based on logistic regression
questions.answer: Six hardcoded grammar rules and a lookup table of a couple of hundred words and suffixes
questions.explanation: That's exactly how the page describes it. Neural networks, decision trees and logistic regression came decades later. The page puts decision trees in the late 1980s, and p.407 puts logistic regression after that.

questions.question: Why did rule-based translation systems fail to generalise beyond handpicked examples?
questions.answer: Words change meaning dramatically with context, and any grammar rule needs countless exceptions, so a small rule set that worked on curated sentences couldn't handle real text robustly.
questions.explanation: The page gives these two reasons explicitly.

questions.question: Why did handcrafted rules remain dominant into the 1990s even though their problems were obvious?
questions.answer: There was no viable alternative. Learning rules from data needed faster computers and more data, which only became available in the late 1980s.
questions.explanation: The page says there was 'simply no viable alternative' until compute and data grew.

questions.question: How does the page's description of the shift to machine learning ('search for the rules within some rule space') match the book's general definition of machine learning?
questions.answer: Both describe ML as an automatic search, guided by data, through a space of possible rules or representations, instead of having a human write the rules.
questions.explanation: Chapter 1 (p.30) frames ML as systematically searching for representations and rules using feedback. This page applies that framing to NLP.

questions.question: What makes natural language 'natural', according to the authors?
options: It is spoken rather than written
It was shaped by an evolutionary process, with usage first and rules later
It is processed by the human brain
questions.answer: It was shaped by an evolutionary process, with usage first and rules later
questions.explanation: The page says natural language evolved much like biological organisms, which is what makes it natural. It does have grammar, but formalised after the fact. Being spoken or processed by the brain isn't the authors' criterion.

questions.question: Can you connect the Georgetown-IBM story to the ML idea of evaluating on held-out data?
questions.answer: The demo was judged on 60 handpicked sentences it was designed for, like evaluating on training data. Real performance on unseen text was far worse, which is why held-out test sets matter.
questions.explanation: This is an interpretation (not stated by the authors) linking the history to evaluation practice taught in chapter 5.

questions.question: What were the earliest machine learning approaches to NLP based on, and what was their aim?
questions.answer: Decision trees, aiming to automate the development of the if/then/else rules that hardcoded language systems used.
questions.explanation: Stated at the bottom of this page and continued at the top of p.407.

questions.question: Which two limitations of LSTMs for NLP does the page name?
options: They couldn't generalise to unseen examples and needed hand-written rules
They struggled with dependencies across long text and were slow and unwieldy to train
They had too few parameters and required linguistic features
They couldn't be used for classification and couldn't be stacked
questions.answer: They struggled with dependencies across long text and were slow and unwieldy to train
questions.explanation: The page says LSTMs generalised far better than previous approaches (so the first option is wrong) but struggled with long chains of text and were slow to train compared with vision models. The page says LSTMs dramatically *increased* parameter counts, and nothing on it suggests they couldn't classify or be stacked.

questions.question: Match each example application on the page with its task name.
questions.answer: Email spam probability → text classification; most likely Russian translation of an English sentence → translation; the next word of an incomplete sentence → language modeling.
questions.explanation: These are the three bullets on the page.

questions.question: What two properties of the Transformer does the page credit for solving the LSTMs' scalability issues?
questions.answer: (1) Its accuracy kept improving as model size and training data increased together. (2) Its training could be parallelised effectively even for long sequences, so doubling the machines roughly halves training time.
questions.explanation: Both are stated in the 'Toward the end of the 2010s' paragraph.

questions.question: What does Jelinek's joke 'Every time I fire a linguist, the performance of the speech recognizer goes up' illustrate?
questions.answer: That hand-built linguistic knowledge baked into a model came to be seen as a hindrance, and that learned parametric models trained on data often outperformed systems with hand-engineered linguistic rules.
questions.explanation: The page uses the quote to illustrate learned models taking over from embedded linguistics.

questions.question: What is the authors' position on whether the book's text models understand language?
options: They have human-like understanding once trained on enough data
They don't understand language; they find statistical regularities, which is enough for many tasks
They understand syntax but not meaning
They can't perform well on real-world tasks
questions.answer: They don't understand language; they find statistical regularities, which is enough for many tasks
questions.explanation: That's stated directly. The first option contradicts the page. The third option's syntax/semantics split isn't the authors' claim. The fourth contradicts 'sufficient to perform well on a wide array of real-world tasks'.

questions.question: Why does the page draw an analogy between computer vision and NLP?
questions.answer: Both are pattern recognition, one on pixels and one on words. That suggests the same deep learning toolkit applies to text once it is turned into numeric tensors, which is the topic of section 14.2.
questions.explanation: The page says 'Much as computer vision is pattern recognition applied to pixels, the modern field of NLP is all about pattern recognition applied to words in text.'

questions.question: Using what you learned about RNNs in chapter 13, can you explain in your own words why an LSTM is hard to parallelise across timesteps?
questions.answer: Each hidden state depends on the previous one ($h_t = f(h_{t-1}, x_t)$), so timesteps must be processed in order. You can't compute step 100 before step 99.
questions.explanation: This connects the page's claim that LSTMs were slow to train with the recurrence mechanism from chapter 13 (p.390). The page itself doesn't give the mechanism.

questions.question: What does re.findall(r".", "Hi there.") return?
questions.explanation: In a regex, "." matches any single character, so every character, including the space and the period, becomes a token. The first option is word-level splitting, the third treats "." as a literal period (that would need \.), and the last wrongly drops the space and period.

questions.question: Why do the authors say images have a "relatively natural numeric representation" while text does not?
questions.answer: Images are already grids of pixel intensities, i.e. numbers. Text is a sequence of discrete symbols, and you must choose how to break it up (characters, words, ...) and how to number the pieces; several valid schemes exist.
questions.explanation: The page states that before modelling "we need to translate the written word into tensors of numbers" and that text can be represented numerically "in several ways."

questions.question: What is a token, according to this page?
questions.answer: A small individual unit that text is split into during the splitting step of preprocessing.
questions.explanation: The book defines splitting as the step "where text is split into small individual units, called tokens."

questions.question: Name the two representations proposed on this page and give one advantage of each.
questions.answer: Character-level (e.g. ASCII-like indices for each character): a small alphabet and no unknown words. Word-level (split on spaces and punctuation): each token carries more meaning and sequences are much shorter.
questions.explanation: The book proposes both and calls them "good approaches to try"; the advantages listed are an elaboration (the book develops the trade-off in 14.2.1-14.2.2).

questions.question: Which statement best matches the authors' view of modern language models on this page?
options: They reason like humans but more efficiently.
They copy and synthesize training data in a way distinct from human intelligence, yet their emergent behaviour is surprising.
They depend on hand-coded linguistic features from the 1990s.
They are no more capable than logistic regression.
questions.answer: They copy and synthesize training data in a way distinct from human intelligence, yet their emergent behaviour is surprising.
questions.explanation: The text says they are "wholly distinct (and much less efficient!)" than human intelligence, but their emergence from "guess the missing word" was "one of the most shocking empirical results." The first option contradicts "less efficient", the third contradicts the move away from hard-coded features, and the fourth contradicts the stated surprise.

questions.question: Without looking, write split_chars from memory, and predict its first five outputs for "The quick brown fox...".
questions.answer: def split_chars(text): return re.findall(r".", text); the first five tokens are "T", "h", "e", " ", "q".
questions.explanation: Check against the code on this page and the output on p.409.

questions.question: What does split_words("Wait, what?") return?
questions.explanation: [\w]+ grabs each word, [.,!?;] grabs "," and "?" as separate tokens, and the space is skipped. The first drops punctuation, the second glues punctuation to words (that would be whitespace splitting), and the fourth is character-level.

questions.question: Why do the authors prefer a vocabulary to ASCII lookups such as ord('A') -> 65?
questions.answer: ASCII/Unicode indexing scales poorly to other languages (Unicode has over a million characters), while a vocabulary maps only the tokens that occur in our data and works equally for words and characters.
questions.explanation: Stated directly in the paragraph beginning "For character tokens...".

questions.question: What two properties of indexing does the page highlight?
questions.answer: It is flexible (it works with a wide range of modelling approaches) and reversible (indices can be mapped back to tokens).
questions.explanation: "This is a flexible and reversible representation of our tokenized input that can work with a wide range of modeling approaches."

questions.question: Which input would split_words handle in a way you might not want?
questions.answer: "isn't"
questions.explanation: The apostrophe is neither a word character nor in [.,!?;], so it is dropped and "isn't" becomes ["isn", "t"]. The others contain only word characters, spaces and listed punctuation, which split cleanly.

questions.question: The example sentence has 45 characters and split_words gives 10 tokens for it. If each token gets a one-hot vector, compare the vector dimension needed for raw Unicode code points with a word vocabulary of the 9 entries on pp.409-410.
questions.answer: Unicode code points would need about 1.1 million dimensions (0..1,114,111), while the vocabulary needs only 9 (indices 0-8).
questions.explanation: One-hot dimension equals the size of the index space. This is the scaling problem the page points to with "over a million characters in the Unicode specification."

questions.question: Explain in your own words the difference between splitting and indexing, and which one decides the latent space.
questions.answer: Splitting turns a string into string tokens; indexing maps tokens to integers. Neither decides the latent space; mapping indices to vectors is a later modelling choice.
questions.explanation: The page: "Later on, we can decide how to map from token indices into a latent space ingested by the model."

questions.question: Why is the FIRST element of [0, 2, 3, 4, 5, 6, 1, 0, 7, 8] equal to 0?
options: "The" is a stop word removed by split_words
"The" is capitalized and the vocabulary only contains lowercase "the"
Indices always start at 0 for the first token
questions.answer: "The" is capitalized and the vocabulary only contains lowercase "the"
questions.explanation: split_words preserves case, and vocabulary.get("The", 0) misses, so it returns the default 0. split_words removes nothing but whitespace; indices are lookups, not positions; and [UNK] is a vocabulary entry, not the word "The".

questions.question: What problem does the [UNK] token solve?
questions.answer: It lets us index all input, even terms not in the vocabulary (e.g. ones that only occur in test data), by mapping them to a reserved index.
questions.explanation: The book: "This way, we can index all input we come across, even if some terms only occur in our test data."

questions.question: Why do the two "sunset" sentences end up with very different index sequences without standardization?
questions.answer: Indexing is exact string matching: "i"/"I", "Mexico"/"México", "isnt"/"isn't" and "staring"/"stared" are different strings and get different (or unknown) indices, and the model doesn't know a priori that they are equivalent.
questions.explanation: This is the argument in the paragraph "They are very similar...".

questions.question: After lowercasing and punctuation removal, which difference between the two sentences remains?
questions.answer: "mexico" vs. "méxico"
questions.explanation: Lowercasing removes case differences and punctuation removal removes the apostrophe and question marks; the accent survives, which is why the book says removing accent marks would bring them even closer.

questions.question: What is stemming or lemmatization, and give the book's examples.
questions.answer: Mapping words to a common root, traditionally with regular expressions: "tired" -> "tire", "trophies" -> "trophy".
questions.explanation: Defined in the last paragraph of the page.

questions.question: Why do the authors call standardization "a basic form of feature engineering"?
questions.answer: Because it is a hand-designed transformation of the input that builds in human knowledge (case or accents don't matter) to make learning easier, instead of letting the model learn it.
questions.explanation: Feature engineering means hand-crafting input transformations; standardization erases differences "you don't want your model to have to deal with."

questions.question: Modify the indexing code mentally so that the output has only one 0. What single change suffices?
questions.answer: Lowercase the input before splitting (e.g. split_words(text.lower())), so that "The" becomes "the" -> 1; only "lazy" remains unknown.
questions.explanation: This is exactly what CharTokenizer/WordTokenizer's standardize step does on pp.411-412.

questions.question: Why does heavy standardization like stemming tend to hurt today's larger models?
options: It makes the vocabulary too large
Tense and plurality are necessary signals to a word's meaning and get erased
It cannot be implemented with regular expressions
Large models cannot process lowercase text
questions.answer: Tense and plurality are necessary signals to a word's meaning and get erased
questions.explanation: The book says exactly this. Stemming shrinks the vocabulary rather than enlarging it, it was historically done with regexes, and lowercase text is no problem for any model.

questions.question: List the three stages of text preprocessing in order and what each produces.
questions.answer: Standardization (normalized text), splitting (a sequence of tokens), indexing (a sequence of integer indices via a vocabulary).
questions.explanation: This is the numbered list and figure 14.1.

questions.question: In figure 14.1, why does "the" map to 3 in both positions?
questions.answer: Indexing is a vocabulary lookup that depends only on the token string, not its position, so the same token always gets the same index.
questions.explanation: The vocabulary maps each distinct token to one index.

questions.question: In CharTokenizer, what happens when index() meets a character not in the vocabulary?
options: It returns self.unk_id for that character
It adds the character to the vocabulary
questions.answer: It returns self.unk_id for that character
questions.explanation: index uses self.vocabulary.get(t, self.unk_id). A KeyError could only occur in __init__ if [UNK] were missing; nothing is skipped and the vocabulary is never modified.

questions.question: What is the only standardization step CharTokenizer applies?
questions.answer: Lowercasing (inputs.lower()).
questions.explanation: "To keep things simple, we will use only one standardization step—we lowercase all input."

questions.question: What is the purpose of defining __call__ in CharTokenizer?
questions.answer: It makes the tokenizer instance callable like a function, so tokenizer(text) runs standardize -> split -> index and returns indices.
questions.explanation: __call__ chains the stage methods; the final index and return lines are on p.412.

questions.question: Can you explain, without notes, the difference between the narrow and the broad meaning of "tokenization"?
questions.answer: Narrow: only the splitting step. Broad (as the book uses it here): the entire standardize-split-index process.
questions.explanation: See the paragraph "People often refer to the entire process as tokenization...".

questions.question: With max_size=100, at most how many distinct characters (excluding [UNK]) does compute_char_vocabulary keep?
questions.explanation: most_common(max_size - len(vocabulary)) with len(vocabulary) = 1 keeps 99 tokens, plus [UNK] = 100 entries. 64 is what Moby Dick actually yields on p.413 (63 characters + [UNK]), because the book has fewer distinct characters than the cap.

questions.question: Which index does the most frequent character get, and why?
questions.answer: Index 1, because [UNK] occupies index 0 and tokens are appended in descending frequency order before enumerate assigns positions.
questions.explanation: vocabulary starts as ["[UNK]"], then most_common's ordered tokens are appended.

questions.question: Why do the authors want to limit vocabulary size?
questions.answer: Because, on the modelling side, limiting vocabulary size is an important way to limit the number of parameters in a model; rare tokens can go to [UNK].
questions.explanation: Stated in the paragraph before Listing 14.2. Layers such as embeddings have one parameter row per vocabulary entry.

questions.question: What is the only difference between Listing 14.1 and Listing 14.3?
questions.answer: The regex in split
questions.explanation: WordTokenizer uses r"[\w]+|[.,!?;]" instead of r".". Both lowercase, both use unk_id, and both return lists of ints.

questions.question: Why does compute_char_vocabulary lowercase and split exactly like CharTokenizer does?
questions.answer: The vocabulary must contain the same token strings the tokenizer will produce; otherwise lookups would miss and many tokens would map to [UNK] (e.g. uppercase letters never present in the vocabulary).
questions.explanation: Consistency between vocabulary building and tokenization is required for correct indexing.

questions.question: An embedding layer has V*d parameters. If you cap a word vocabulary at 2,000 instead of the about 17,000 words needed for all of Moby Dick (p.414), with d = 64, how many parameters do you save?
questions.explanation: Parameters scale linearly with V: 17,000*64 = 1,088,000 vs. 2,000*64 = 128,000. This illustrates the page's point that vocabulary size limits parameter count (the embedding formula is not on this page).

questions.question: Trace compute_char_vocabulary(["aba"], max_size=3) by hand. What dict comes out?
questions.explanation: Counts: a:2, b:1; most_common(2) gives [(a,2),(b,1)]; with [UNK] first, enumerate gives 0, 1, 2.

questions.question: Why is the character vocabulary length 64 rather than 100?
options: compute_char_vocabulary drops the 36 least common characters
Only 63 distinct lowercase characters occur in the text, plus [UNK]
questions.answer: Only 63 distinct lowercase characters occur in the text, plus [UNK]
questions.explanation: most_common(99) returns at most as many items as there are distinct tokens. Nothing is dropped below the cap, max_size is respected, and Keras plays no role in the vocabulary function.

questions.question: What is the single change from Listing 14.2 to Listing 14.4 (apart from variable names)?
questions.answer: The split regex: r"[\w]+|[.,!?;]" instead of r".".
questions.explanation: The page says "We can also substitute this new split rule into our vocabulary function."

questions.question: Why are the first entries of the vocabulary [UNK], space, e, t, a, o, ...?
questions.answer: [UNK] is placed at index 0 by construction; the rest are appended in descending frequency from most_common, and in English text the space and letters e, t, a, o are the most frequent characters.
questions.explanation: Dict insertion order preserves that ranking when listing keys.

questions.question: The opening line has 63 characters and becomes 63 character tokens. If a word tokenizer produced 13 tokens for it, what is the compression ratio, and roughly how many characters per word-token is that?
questions.answer: 63 / 13 is about 4.8, so roughly 4.8 characters per word token (spaces included).
questions.explanation: Sequence length shrinks by the average number of characters each word token stands for. The 13 comes from applying the word regex in these notes; check p.414 for the book's printed result.

questions.question: What does keras.utils.get_file return in this code?
options: The text contents of the file
The local path to the downloaded (cached) file
questions.answer: The local path to the downloaded (cached) file
questions.explanation: The result is passed to open(filename, "r"), so it is a path. The list of lines comes from list(open(...)), and no Dataset is created.

questions.question: What would happen if you passed a vocabulary built by compute_char_vocabulary to WordTokenizer?
questions.answer: Almost every word token would be missing from the character vocabulary and map to [UNK] (only single-letter words and the punctuation marks would match), making the encoding useless.
questions.explanation: The vocabulary must be built with the same split rule as the tokenizer, which is why Listing 14.4 exists.

questions.question: Predict, before reading p.414, how the word-level vocabulary size and sequence length for Moby Dick will compare with the character-level results here.
questions.answer: A much larger vocabulary (thousands of words; it fills a 2,000 cap, and about 17,000 would be needed for the whole book) but much shorter sequences.
questions.explanation: This is exactly the comparison drawn on p.414.

questions.question: On Moby Dick, which pair of numbers describes the word-level tokenizer built on this page?
questions.answer: Vocabulary 2,000, line length 13
questions.explanation: The printout shows Vocabulary length: 2000 and Line length: 13. 64/63 are the character tokenizer's numbers (p.413). 17,000 is how many terms full coverage would take, not the capped vocabulary. 16 is the subword tokenizer's line length (p.418).

questions.question: Why is "[UNK]" the first entry of the vocabulary, and why does ',' come right after it?
questions.answer: compute_word_vocabulary inserts "[UNK]" first (index 0) and then appends tokens in descending frequency order; the comma is the most frequent token in the book.
questions.explanation: Listing 14.4 starts with vocabulary = ["[UNK]"] and then loops over most_common(max_size - 1). Dicts preserve insertion order, so keys() reflects frequency rank.

questions.question: Explain the trade-off between vocabulary size and sequence length using the numbers on this page and p.413.
questions.answer: Characters: 64 terms give full coverage but 63 tokens for the test line. Words: 13 tokens, but the 2,000-term vocabulary is full and covers only part of the ~17,000 distinct words, so the rest become "[UNK]". Lowering one quantity raises the other.
questions.explanation: The page states that a character tokenizer 'needs only 64 vocabulary terms ... but will encode each input as a very long sequence', while a word tokenizer 'quickly fills a 2,000-term vocabulary' with 'much shorter' outputs.

questions.question: According to the authors, what happens if you aggressively restrict a word-level vocabulary on a huge dataset?
options: Much text is encoded as "[UNK]", throwing out valuable information
The model can no longer handle punctuation
Training becomes impossible because the embedding grows
questions.answer: Much text is encoded as "[UNK]", throwing out valuable information
questions.explanation: The page says exactly this. Sequence length doesn't grow from capping (each word is still one token). Punctuation is handled by the regex. A growing embedding is the problem with *not* restricting the vocabulary.

questions.question: Using cost ≈ L·log2(V) bits (an approximation added in these notes, not from the book), compare the character and word encodings of the test sentence.
questions.explanation: The word encoding is about 2.6x more compact by this measure, but it is lossy for words outside the top 2,000. Subword tokenization aims to approach the word figure without losing information.

questions.question: Why does the word tokenizer give 13 tokens for "Call me Ishmael. Some years ago--never mind how long precisely."? What happens to the '--'?
questions.answer: The regex [\w]+|[.,!?;] yields 11 words plus 2 periods = 13 tokens; '--' matches neither alternative, so it is silently dropped.
questions.explanation: Tokens: call, me, ishmael, ., some, years, ago, never, mind, how, long, precisely, . The hyphen isn't a word character and isn't in the punctuation class.

questions.question: In what sense is choosing a tokenizer a compression problem, according to section 14.2.2?
questions.answer: Shorter token sequences compress each example's length, and a smaller vocabulary reduces the bytes needed per token; achieving both produces short, information-rich sequences for the model.
questions.explanation: This is the page's final paragraph. It sets up byte-pair encoding, a compression algorithm, on p.415.

questions.question: Can you state the two properties subword tokenization tries to combine, and which existing tokenizer supplies each?
questions.answer: Concise output (from WordTokenizer) and encoding a wide range of inputs with a small vocabulary (from CharTokenizer).
questions.explanation: Taken directly from the first paragraph of 14.2.2.

questions.question: What is the starting vocabulary in byte-pair encoding, as described on this page?
questions.answer: A basic vocabulary of characters
questions.explanation: The page says BPE 'start[s] with a basic vocabulary of characters and progressively merge[s] common pairings'. Word vocabularies are the WordTokenizer approach. BPE doesn't enumerate all byte pairs up front, and it doesn't start empty.

questions.question: Why does count_and_split_words join the characters of each word with spaces?
questions.answer: To make pairs of adjacent symbols easy to find in the next step: word.split() gives the symbols, and a merge becomes a substitution of "a b" with "ab".
questions.explanation: The page states the spaces 'make it easier to consider pairs of characters in our next step'. Listing 14.6 on p.416 relies on this.

questions.question: What would count_and_split_words return if the corpus contained the line "The fox-hound!"?
questions.answer: Entries "t h e", "f o x", "h o u n d" and "!" each incremented by 1; the hyphen is dropped by the regex.
questions.explanation: The line is lowercased, and r"[\w]+|[.,!?;]" yields 'the', 'fox', 'hound', '!'. '-' matches neither alternative. A single-character token like '!' stays as "!" with no spaces.

questions.question: Using the counts printed on this page, which adjacent pair has the highest total frequency?
questions.explanation: (o,w) appears in "b r o w n" (×3) and "s l o w" (×1) = 4. (t,h), (f,o) and (b,r) each total 3. This matches the first merge on p.416.

questions.question: Where did byte-pair encoding come from originally, according to the page?
questions.answer: It is a 1990s algorithm for lossless data compression (Philip Gage, 'A New Algorithm for Data Compression', The C Users Journal, 1994).
questions.explanation: Stated in the first paragraph and footnote 1.

questions.question: Why is storing counts per distinct word more efficient than processing the raw corpus for every merge?
questions.answer: Each round of pair counting only needs to visit each distinct word once and multiply by its frequency, instead of rescanning every occurrence in the text.
questions.explanation: For Moby Dick that means about 17k keys (p.414) instead of hundreds of thousands of word occurrences.

questions.question: Can you write down from memory the counts dict for the toy corpus and explain each value?
questions.answer: {"t h e": 3, "q u i c k": 2, "b r o w n": 3, "f o x": 2, "s l o w": 1, "f o x h o u n d": 1}
questions.explanation: Count each word across the three lines: 'the' and 'brown' appear in every line; 'quick' and 'fox' in two; 'slow' and 'foxhound' in one.

questions.question: Why is ("o", "w") the first pair merged?
options: It appears in the most distinct words of any pair
Its frequency-weighted count, 4, is the highest
It is alphabetically first among ties
questions.answer: Its frequency-weighted count, 4, is the highest
questions.explanation: brown (×3) + slow (×1) = 4, more than any other pair (several have 3). Counting distinct words isn't the criterion (o,w is in only two words). There is no vowel rule. Ties are broken by insertion order, not alphabetically, and there is no tie here anyway.

questions.question: What does the regex (?<!\S)first second(?!\S) ensure in merge_pair?
questions.answer: That the pair is matched only as two complete symbols, preceded and followed by a space or the string boundary, not as part of a longer symbol.
questions.explanation: The lookbehind and lookahead forbid a non-space character directly before or after the match. The callout calls this matching an 'unmerged pair'.

questions.question: In the state after merge 6 ("the", "q u i c k", "brown", "f o x", "s l ow", "f o x h o u n d"), what is the count of ("f","o"), and why is it merged next?
questions.answer: 3: 2 from 'f o x' (fox ×2) plus 1 from 'f o x h o u n d' (foxhound ×1). It ties with (o,x) at 3 and is counted first, and every other pair is ≤ 2.
questions.explanation: count_pairs weights pairs by word frequency; max() returns the first key with the maximal value.

questions.question: Why does 'foxhound' end up as "fox h o u n d" while 'fox' becomes a single symbol?
questions.answer: The pairs inside 'fox' are frequent (they occur in fox ×2 and foxhound ×1), but the pairs in 'hound' occur only once, so they never win a merge within ten steps.
questions.explanation: The page's conclusion: common words are merged entirely, less common words only partially.

questions.question: How many new vocabulary entries do the ten iterations of the loop create?
options: It depends on the number of words
questions.explanation: Each merge creates one new symbol (ow, th, the, br, brow, brown, fo, fox, qu, qui). 'the, brown, fox' are just the complete words among them.

questions.question: What would happen to the loop if all words became single symbols before the 10 iterations ended?
questions.answer: count_pairs would return an empty Counter and max() would raise a ValueError.
questions.explanation: Beyond the book: Listing 14.6 has no guard; in practice you stop when no pairs remain or the target vocabulary size is reached.

questions.question: Can you predict the 11th merge on the toy data?
questions.answer: ("qui", "c") with count 2, giving "quic k".
questions.explanation: After merge 10 the remaining count-2 pairs are (qui,c) and (c,k); (qui,c) is counted first. All other pairs have count 1.

questions.question: In bpe_merge, which pair is merged at each step?
options: The most frequent pair in the input word
The pair with the lowest rank in self.merges
A random pair from the vocabulary
questions.answer: The pair with the lowest rank in self.merges
questions.explanation: best = min(pairs, key=lambda pair: self.merges.get(pair, 1e9)). The callout says merge rules are applied in rank order. Frequency in the input word isn't used. The leftmost pair is only chosen if it has the lowest rank. Nothing is random.

questions.question: What are the two conditions under which bpe_merge stops?
questions.answer: (1) No pairs remain (the word is a single symbol); (2) the best pair is not in self.merges, meaning no learned rule applies to any present pair.
questions.explanation: The two `break` statements in the printed loop.

questions.question: Why does the vocabulary start with all characters of the training text, and what does that guarantee?
questions.answer: So any word made of those characters can be encoded, at worst one character per token. That guarantees no [UNK] on text using the training character set.
questions.explanation: p.418 confirms: the vocabulary contains every character in the source text, so the worst case is tokenizing a word into individual characters.

questions.question: Why does the pair search use overlapped=True?
questions.answer: Adjacent pairs share symbols ('b r', 'r o', 'o w'); a normal findall would skip every other pair, so the lowest-rank pair might be missed.
questions.explanation: overlapped is a feature of the third-party regex module, which the chapter imports as re on p.408.

questions.question: If the training corpus contains 60 distinct characters and vocab_size = 2,000, how many merges does compute_sub_word_vocabulary learn (assuming pairs never run out)?
questions.explanation: Each merge adds exactly one vocabulary entry on top of [UNK] and the base characters (structure per the page's description; the exact character count for Moby Dick isn't given on this page).

questions.question: Which parts of Listing 14.7 are missing in the printed book, and how can you tell?
questions.answer: After `vocab = ["[` the code jumps into the middle of bpe_merge: the end of the training function, the class definition, __init__, standardize and the start of bpe_merge are missing. In split, the regex after r"[ and the line joining characters with a space (the target of the 'Joins all characters with a space' callout) are also missing.
questions.explanation: The indentation jumps from function level to deep inside a method, a stray '<' appears, and a callout points at a blank line.

questions.question: Using the toy ranks from p.416, can you tokenize 'flow'?
questions.answer: 'f l o w' → merge 'o w' (rank 0) → 'f l ow'; pairs 'f l' and 'l ow' have no rules → tokens f, l, ow.
questions.explanation: Only learned merges apply, in rank order.

questions.question: Why does the subword vocabulary start with "e", "t", "a", "o", ... right after [UNK]?
options: They are the first merges learned
Base characters are added first, sorted by frequency
They are alphabetically sorted vowels and consonants
The tokenizer reserves IDs for single letters at random
questions.answer: Base characters are added first, sorted by frequency
questions.explanation: compute_sub_word_vocabulary builds char_counts and uses most_common() (p.417). Merges come after the characters. The order is by frequency, not alphabetical, and nothing is random.

questions.question: What is the worst-case tokenization of a word by the SubWordTokenizer, and why?
questions.answer: One token per character, because the vocabulary contains every character and bpe_merge simply stops when no learned merge applies.
questions.explanation: Stated on the page; follows from the vocabulary initialization on p.417.

questions.question: The subword tokenizer uses 16 tokens where the word tokenizer uses 13. Why do the authors still call this an advantage?
questions.answer: With the same 2,000-term vocabulary it achieves near-word-level average length while never needing [UNK], so no information is lost on rare words.
questions.explanation: 'We have achieved a short average token length while handling rare words with a small vocabulary.'

questions.question: Why is the slower training of the subword vocabulary rarely a concern?
options: A vocabulary is learned once per model and costs little compared with model training
The merges are cached by Keras
Only the first 100 merges are needed
questions.answer: A vocabulary is learned once per model and costs little compared with model training
questions.explanation: This is the page's argument. The toy implementation is pure Python on the CPU, Keras plays no role in it, and all ~1,900+ merges are used.

questions.question: According to the sidebar, why is the tokenization question trivial for a pretrained model?
questions.answer: You must preserve the exact tokenization used during pretraining; otherwise the model's learned representations of input tokens are thrown away.
questions.explanation: Sidebar on p.418, continued on p.419.

questions.question: Some vocabulary-end entries are whole words ('pilot'), others fragments ('ilo'). What does that tell you about how BPE builds a vocabulary?
questions.answer: BPE adds whatever frequent adjacent pairs exist, regardless of linguistic meaning. Some merges complete words, others create pieces shared by many words.
questions.explanation: Merges are driven only by pair frequency (p.416), so fragments appear whenever they are common across words.

questions.question: Can you fill in the comparison table (vocabulary size, tokens for the test line, [UNK] usage) for the three tokenizers from memory?
questions.answer: Char: 64 / 63 / none. Word: 2,000 / 13 / many rare words. Subword: 2,000 / 16 / none.

questions.question: Why must you keep a pretrained model's tokenization?
options: Otherwise you throw out the token representations learned in the model weights
Because Keras only supports one tokenizer per model
Because pretrained models only accept characters
questions.answer: Otherwise you throw out the token representations learned in the model weights
questions.explanation: Stated in the sidebar. Speed and Keras limitations aren't the reason, and pretrained models typically use subword, not character, tokenization.

questions.question: According to the sidebar, why does shorter average input length improve performance?
questions.answer: A model can better track long-range dependencies in the text when inputs are shorter.
questions.explanation: This is the stated reason the compression offered by word and subword tokenizers is 'too important to pass up'.

questions.question: Give one task suited to character-level tokenization and one advantage of word-level tokenization, as named on this page.
questions.answer: Spelling correction may benefit from characters. Word-level is simple and interpretable, since each input is a word a human would read, which makes ranking tokens by importance to a prediction easy.
questions.explanation: Both come from the 'no one-size-fits-all' paragraph of the sidebar.

questions.question: Which statement about the Transformer matches the page?
options: It processes words strictly one at a time
It discards word order like a bag-of-words model
It is technically order-agnostic but injects word-position information
It cannot be called a sequence model
questions.answer: It is technically order-agnostic but injects word-position information
questions.explanation: The page calls it a hybrid. Strictly sequential processing describes RNNs. It doesn't discard order, because position information is added. The page explicitly calls RNNs and Transformers sequence models.

questions.question: Why is representing individual tokens called 'relatively uncontroversial'?
questions.answer: Tokens are categorical features from a predefined set (the vocabulary), and we know how to encode those, as feature-space dimensions or category (token) vectors.
questions.explanation: The difficulty lies in encoding order, not in encoding single tokens.

questions.question: How does the page argue that word order in language differs from order in a timeseries?
questions.answer: Words have no natural, canonical order: languages (English vs. Japanese) order similar words differently, the same thing can be said with reshuffled words, and even a randomized short sentence can sometimes be understood. Order matters, but its relationship to meaning isn't straightforward.
questions.explanation: Taken from the second paragraph of 14.3.

questions.question: Which models does the page call 'sequence models'?
questions.answer: RNNs and Transformers
questions.explanation: 'Because they take into account word order, both RNNs and Transformers are called sequence models.' Bag-of-words discards order.

questions.question: Can you place a bigram model on the order spectrum described here (discard / strict order / hybrid)?
questions.answer: It is still a set model, but it keeps a little local order by treating pairs of consecutive tokens as features.
questions.explanation: See 14.4.2 (p.427) and the chapter summary (p.443): bigram or trigram models consider the presence or absence of two or three consecutive tokens.

questions.question: According to the page, when did interest in sequence models for NLP start rising?
options: In the 1990s, with the invention of LSTMs
In 2015, with the rebirth of RNNs
questions.answer: In 2015, with the rebirth of RNNs
questions.explanation: The text says interest in sequence models 'only started rising in 2015, with the rebirth of RNNs.' LSTMs date from the 1990s but did not trigger that rise; the Transformer came later; AlexNet is a computer-vision milestone.

questions.question: What does the `unsup/` directory contain, and why must it be excluded when building the labeled training set?
questions.answer: Reviews the dataset creator deliberately left unlabeled (they may be positive or negative). A directory-based loader would otherwise treat `unsup` as a third class.
questions.explanation: The page defines unsup/ as unlabeled reviews; p.421 ignores them for now, and p.438 later uses them for pretraining.

questions.question: How does the IMDb data used on this page differ from the version used in chapter 4, and what extra work does that create?
questions.answer: Chapter 4's version was prevectorized: reviews were already integer word-index sequences with a fixed vocabulary. Here you get raw text files, so you must read files, take labels from folders, split off validation data, choose a tokenizer and vectorize.
questions.explanation: The page contrasts the prevectorized chapter 4/5 data with raw text 'just like you would do when approaching a new text-classification problem in the real world' (see also p.130).

questions.question: What does `extract=True` do in `keras.utils.get_file` in Listing 14.8?
options: It unpacks the downloaded archive after downloading
It splits off a validation set
questions.answer: It unpacks the downloaded archive after downloading
questions.explanation: `extract=True` makes get_file unpack the tar.gz so the aclImdb folder appears on disk. Tokenization, validation splitting and ignoring unsup all happen in later steps.

questions.question: Why might a bag-of-words model, which ignores word order, still be a strong choice for movie-review sentiment?
questions.answer: Much of the sentiment signal comes from which words appear ('awful', 'brilliant'), so presence alone is very informative. Order mainly helps with negation and contrast.
questions.explanation: The page says both approaches remain relevant. The explanation of why is our own reasoning and is tested empirically in sections 14.4 and 14.5.

questions.question: How are review labels stored in the raw aclImdb dataset?
options: In a CSV file of filename,label pairs
As the first line of each review file
By the directory the file is in (pos/ or neg/)
They are not available; the dataset is unlabeled
questions.answer: By the directory the file is in (pos/ or neg/)
questions.explanation: Low-rated reviews were sorted into neg/ and high-rated ones into pos/. There is no separate label file, and only unsup/ is unlabeled.

questions.question: Before reading on, open one file from train/pos and one from train/neg. What preprocessing problems do you notice, such as markup or length?
questions.answer:
Open-ended. Typical observations: HTML line breaks (
), mixed case, punctuation, and very variable lengths.
questions.explanation: This follows the page's advice to inspect your data before modeling; p.421 prints one such review.

questions.question: Each IMDb training class has 12,500 reviews. With val_percentage = 0.2, how many reviews end up in imdb_train and imdb_val in total?
questions.explanation: int(12500 × 0.2) = 2500 per class go to validation, and the remaining 10,000 per class go to training. Page 422 confirms 20,000 train and 5,000 validation reviews.

questions.question: Why does Listing 14.10 use random.Random(1337).shuffle instead of an unseeded shuffle?
options: So that the same files land in the validation set on every run
Because os.listdir returns files in random order
To balance positive and negative reviews
questions.answer: So that the same files land in the validation set on every run
questions.explanation: A fixed seed makes the split reproducible. It does not affect speed. os.listdir order is arbitrary but not random. Class balance comes from looping over the classes separately, not from the seed.

questions.question: How does Listing 14.10 make sure that the unsupervised reviews do not appear in the new datasets?
questions.answer: It loops only over the categories ("neg", "pos"), so files in train/unsup are never copied. The test folder has no unsup subfolder.
questions.explanation: The body text says the unsupervised reviews are ignored for now. This is implemented simply by choosing which categories to copy.

questions.question: Why split each class separately instead of shuffling all 25,000 training files together and taking 20%?
questions.answer: Splitting per class guarantees that the validation set has exactly the same 50/50 class ratio as the training data. A pooled shuffle would be only approximately balanced.
questions.explanation: This is our reading of the loop structure; the book does not state the reason explicitly.

questions.question: What does shutil.copytree(imdb_extract_dir / "test", test_dir) do?
options: Moves the test folder and deletes the original
Recursively copies the test folder, unchanged, to imdb_test
Splits the test folder into test and validation
questions.answer: Recursively copies the test folder, unchanged, to imdb_test
questions.explanation: copytree copies a whole directory tree. The original stays (despite the callout's word 'Moves'). The test data is not split, and the folder is not empty.

questions.question: Name two kinds of noise visible in the review printed by Listing 14.9.
questions.answer:
Any two of: HTML line-break tags (
), misspellings or wrong words ('hole' for 'whole', 'there' for 'their'), inconsistent capitalization (lowercase 'i'), run-on sentences.
questions.explanation: All are visible in the printed text and affect how tokenization and standardization should be designed.

questions.question: Can you explain in your own words how text_dataset_from_directory will know which reviews are positive and which are negative?
questions.answer: From the folder names: each subdirectory (neg, pos) becomes a class, and the label is the index of the folder in alphanumeric order (neg = 0, pos = 1).
questions.explanation: The page links it to image_dataset_from_directory from chapter 8, which uses the same directory-to-label convention.

questions.question: Using the page's vocabulary, what is the multi-hot vector for "film made me laugh"?
questions.explanation: film→2, made→3, me→0 ([UNK]), laugh→4, so the set is {0,2,3,4}. Option 2 forgets that 'me' turns on [UNK]. Option 3 is the page's original sentence. Option 4 wrongly includes 'cry'.

questions.question: Why does token ID 0 appear twice in [0, 1, 3, 0, 5] but only once in the set?
questions.answer: Both 'this' and 'me' are out of vocabulary and map to [UNK] = 0. A set keeps each element only once.
questions.explanation: Converting to a set removes order and duplicates.

questions.question: With batch_size = 32, how many batches make up one epoch over train_ds?
questions.answer: ceil(20000 / 32) = 625 batches.
questions.explanation: train_ds holds 20,000 reviews (p.422), and 20000/32 = 625 exactly.

questions.question: Why does the book say 'terrible' would probably, though not always, indicate a bad review? What limitation of set models does this point to?
questions.answer: Context can flip a word's meaning ('not terrible', 'terribly good'). A set model gives each word a single weight regardless of neighbors, so it cannot capture this.
questions.explanation: This motivates bigrams (p.427) and sequence models (p.429).

questions.question: What is the length of a multi-hot vector in a bag-of-words model?
options: The number of tokens in the review
The number of distinct tokens in the review
questions.answer: The vocabulary size
questions.explanation: The vector has one slot per vocabulary entry. Review length and the number of distinct tokens only determine how many slots are 1, and batch size is a separate axis.

questions.question: What do the Datasets from Listing 14.11 yield: token IDs or raw text?
questions.answer: Raw review strings paired with integer labels (neg = 0, pos = 1). Tokenization comes later with TextVectorization.
questions.explanation: text_dataset_from_directory only reads files and labels them; p.423 adds vectorization.

questions.question: Can you write, without looking, the four representations of "this movie made me cry" from this page?
questions.explanation: If you can reproduce them, you understand tokenization, OOV mapping, set conversion and multi-hot encoding.

questions.question: Why does Listing 14.12 call train_ds.map(lambda x, y: x) before adapt()?
options: Because adapt() needs only the text, not the labels
To speed up training of the model
questions.answer: Because adapt() needs only the text, not the labels
questions.explanation: adapt() builds the vocabulary from strings, so the labels must be stripped. The map does not shuffle, does not split data, and is not related to model training speed.

questions.question: What are the shapes of x for one batch from bag_of_words_train_ds, and what does each dimension mean?
questions.answer: (32, 20000): 32 reviews per batch × 20,000 vocabulary slots (presence flags).
questions.explanation: batch_size=32 comes from Listing 14.11 and max_tokens=20,000 from Listing 14.12.

questions.question: Why should adapt() be run on the training set only, and not on validation or test data?
questions.answer: The vocabulary is derived from data. Fitting it on held-out data would let information from those sets influence preprocessing (leakage), and the validation and test sets should simulate unseen data.
questions.explanation: The listing adapts on train_ds_no_labels only and reuses the fitted layer for val and test.

questions.question: Which TextVectorization argument makes the output a presence vector rather than a sequence of token IDs?
questions.answer: output_mode="multi_hot"
questions.explanation: output_mode controls the encoding. split chooses word-level tokenization, max_tokens caps the vocabulary, and num_parallel_calls is an argument of Dataset.map, not of the layer.

questions.question: A linear model on these inputs has one weight per vocabulary entry plus a bias. How many parameters is that, and how many float32 values does one input batch contain?
questions.answer: 20,000 + 1 = 20,001 parameters. One batch has 32 × 20,000 = 640,000 values.
questions.explanation: p.424 confirms the 20,001 parameters. The batch size follows from the printed x.shape.

questions.question: In [1, 1, 0, 1, 0, 1], which word does the 'fifth position' refer to, and is it present?
questions.answer: 'laugh' (index 4); it is absent (0).
questions.explanation: The book counts positions from 1, so the fifth position is index 4 of the vocabulary {[UNK]:0, movie:1, film:2, made:3, laugh:4, cry:5}.

questions.question: Could you swap split="whitespace" for split="character" and predict what the multi-hot vectors would look like? Would that be a good idea for sentiment?
questions.answer: Each vector would mark which characters appear, and almost every review contains nearly every letter, so the vectors would be nearly identical. That is a poor idea, as p.426 notes.
questions.explanation: p.426 explains that a bag of characters tells you very little about a review's content.

questions.question: If max_tokens were 30,000, how many parameters would build_linear_classifier produce?
questions.explanation: One weight per input feature plus one bias. This matches the bigram model on p.428.

questions.question: What does restore_best_weights=True do in the EarlyStopping callback?
options: Saves the model to disk at each epoch
Restores the weights from the epoch with the best monitored val_loss when training stops
Re-initializes the weights when the loss increases
Lowers the learning rate when progress stalls
questions.answer: Restores the weights from the epoch with the best monitored val_loss when training stops
questions.explanation: As the page says, it restores the weights from the best epoch. Saving to disk is ModelCheckpoint, re-initializing is not a Keras behavior, and lowering the learning rate is ReduceLROnPlateau.

questions.question: Why is the 78.13 KB in the model summary consistent with 20,001 parameters?
questions.answer: 20,001 float32 values × 4 bytes = 80,004 bytes, and 80,004 / 1024 ≈ 78.13 KB.
questions.explanation: Keras reports sizes in units of 1024 bytes.

questions.question: Why does the book call this model 'linear' even though it has a sigmoid activation?
questions.answer: The pre-activation score is a linear (affine) function $w^\top x + b$ of the inputs. The sigmoid is a monotonic squashing at the output, so the decision boundary $w^\top x + b = 0$ is a hyperplane.
questions.explanation: There are no hidden layers or nonlinear feature interactions, so the model is logistic regression.

questions.question: Why is the model-building code wrapped in a function?
options: Functions train faster than inline code
So the same architecture can be reused later, for example with a different vocabulary size
Because keras.Model must be created inside a function
questions.answer: So the same architecture can be reused later, for example with a different vocabulary size
questions.explanation: The page says it is saved as a function 'so we can use it again later' (the bigram model on p.428). Wrapping does not affect speed, Keras has no such requirement, and each call creates new weights rather than shared ones.

questions.question: With patience=2 and epochs=10, suppose val_loss is lowest at epoch 3 and never improves afterwards. At which epoch does training stop, and which weights does the model end with?
questions.answer: It stops after epoch 5 (two epochs without improvement) and ends with the epoch-3 weights.
questions.explanation: Patience counts consecutive non-improving epochs (4 and 5), and restore_best_weights reloads epoch 3.

questions.question: Can you explain how one weight of this model relates to one specific English word?
questions.answer: Weight i multiplies input i, which is 1 exactly when vocabulary word i is in the review. So weight i is that word's additive contribution to the log-odds of a positive review.
questions.explanation: This is why the authors value word-level tokens for this model (p.426).

questions.question: According to the page, which part of training the bag-of-words model is most expensive?
options: Tokenizing and encoding the input text
questions.answer: Tokenizing and encoding the input text
questions.explanation: The authors say tokenization and encoding are quite a bit more expensive than updating the model parameters. The parameter update is tiny, validation is a forward pass of the same small model, and plotting happens after training.

questions.question: Figure 14.2 shows 9 epochs, but fit was called with epochs=10. Why?
questions.answer: The EarlyStopping callback (patience=2 on val_loss) stopped training after two epochs without improvement, so the run ended after epoch 9.
questions.explanation: The callback was passed via callbacks=[early_stopping]. Our inference is that the best val_loss was at epoch 7.

questions.question: How does figure 14.2 differ from a classic overfitting curve, and what explanation do the authors give?
questions.answer: In classic overfitting, validation accuracy peaks and then declines. Here it levels off around 0.89 while training accuracy keeps rising. The authors explain that the model is so simple it cannot really overfit.
questions.explanation: The page states this directly.

questions.question: In the plotting code, what does the format string "r--" specify?
options: A red dotted line with markers
questions.answer: A red dashed line
questions.explanation: In matplotlib, 'r' is red and '--' is dashed. It is used for training accuracy, while "b" gives a blue solid line for validation.

questions.question: If the final validation accuracy is about 0.89 on the 5,000-review validation set, roughly how many reviews are misclassified?
questions.explanation: Accuracy is the fraction correct; the validation set has 5,000 reviews (p.422).

questions.question: EarlyStopping monitors val_loss, but the figure plots accuracy. Why might these disagree about the 'best' epoch?
questions.answer: Loss measures the confidence of predictions, while accuracy only counts thresholded decisions. Val_loss can rise (overconfident wrong predictions) while val_accuracy stays flat or rises slightly, so the best epochs can differ.
questions.explanation: Beyond the book; this is why plotting val_loss as well is informative.

questions.question: Before turning the page, predict the test accuracy of this model from figure 14.2.
questions.answer: Close to the validation plateau, about 0.88–0.89. The book reports 0.88388 on p.426.
questions.explanation: Validation accuracy is a good estimate of test accuracy when the validation set has not been heavily tuned on.

questions.question: What test accuracy does listing 14.15 report for the bag-of-words model, and what does model.evaluate return?
questions.answer: 0.88388 (about 88%). model.evaluate returns the loss and the compiled metrics, here [test_loss, test_acc].
questions.explanation: The model was compiled with loss="binary_crossentropy" and metrics=["accuracy"] (p.424), so evaluate returns those two values in that order; the printed accuracy is 0.88388.

questions.question: Why do the authors avoid character-level tokenization for the bag-of-words model?
options: Character vocabularies are too large to fit in memory
A bag of all the characters in a review tells you very little about its content
Character tokenization cannot run on a CPU
questions.answer: A bag of all the characters in a review tells you very little about its content
questions.explanation: That is the reason given on the page. Character vocabularies are tiny (about 64 terms for Moby Dick, p.414), so the first option is wrong. TextVectorization does support character splitting (p.423), and all tokenization runs on the CPU anyway.

questions.question: Why must text preprocessing run on a CPU, and what are the two options for when to do it?
questions.answer: GPUs only handle numeric inputs, so strings must be turned into integer tokens before the train step. You can precompute and save the token IDs before training (possible because tokenization doesn't depend on the model weights), or tokenize on the fly as data is streamed in.
questions.explanation: The sidebar adds that on-the-fly tokenization allows faster experimentation and is required at inference time, where unseen inputs can't be pre-tokenized.

questions.question: According to the sidebar, when does making your tokenizer faster stop helping training speed?
options: When the vocabulary has more than 20,000 terms
When the GPU always has a new preprocessed batch ready, so the GPU is the bottleneck
When you switch from JAX to TensorFlow
questions.answer: When the GPU always has a new preprocessed batch ready, so the GPU is the bottleneck
questions.explanation: Preprocessing only needs to be "fast enough". Vocabulary size and backend choice are not the criterion, and the last option contradicts the page.

questions.question: A GPU step takes 12 ms. One CPU worker needs 60 ms to vectorize a batch. Assuming perfect parallelism and prefetching, what is the minimum num_parallel_calls that makes the GPU the bottleneck?
questions.answer: 5 workers (60/5 = 12 ms ≤ 12 ms).
questions.explanation: With k workers, CPU time per batch is about 60/k ms. We need 60/k ≤ 12, so k ≥ 5. This applies the "fast enough" idea from the sidebar (the arithmetic model is an AI-added simplification).

questions.question: The chapter uses tf.data, yet the authors say the code is multi-backend. Which backend generated the chapter's outputs, and how does Keras make this work?
questions.answer: JAX. Keras automatically converts the input tensors coming out of tf.data to the right format for the active backend (PyTorch, JAX or TensorFlow).
questions.explanation: Stated in the last paragraph of the sidebar.

questions.question: Can you explain, in your own words, why a 20,001-parameter model trained on a CPU is the right first experiment, and what number the following models must beat?
questions.answer: It is cheap, fast, can't really overfit (p.425), and gives an interpretable baseline of about 88% test accuracy that the bigram and sequence models must improve on.
questions.explanation: Check that you can relate the parameter count (p.424), the plateauing validation curve (p.425) and the 0.88388 test accuracy.

questions.question: List the bigrams of "this movie made me cry".
questions.answer: "this movie", "movie made", "made me", "me cry"
questions.explanation: Bigrams are the pairs of consecutive tokens; a five-token sentence has 5 - 2 + 1 = 4 of them, as printed on the page.

questions.question: What does setting ngrams=2 in listing 14.16 do?
options: Keeps only bigrams in the vocabulary
Considers all unigrams and bigrams as vocabulary candidates
Splits each word into two-character pieces
questions.answer: Considers all unigrams and bigrams as vocabulary candidates
questions.explanation: The callout on the listing says "Considers all unigrams and bigrams". Bigrams are word pairs, not character pieces, and the vocabulary size is set explicitly by max_tokens=30_000.

questions.question: Why should "not bad" and "bad" get different sentiment scores, and why can a unigram model not achieve this cleanly?
questions.answer: "Not" reverses the meaning of "bad". A unigram model adds independent word weights, so "not bad" scores w(not) + w(bad), still dominated by the negative "bad". A bigram feature gives the phrase its own weight.
questions.explanation: The page uses this example to argue that discarding all word order is very reductive.

questions.question: Why was max_tokens raised from 20,000 to 30,000?
questions.answer: To account for bigrams, which compete with unigrams for vocabulary slots; a larger vocabulary keeps the common words while adding frequent phrases.
questions.explanation: The text: "We will train a slightly larger vocabulary to account for the presence of bigrams."

questions.question: In a vocabulary where unigrams and bigrams compete for space, when does "United States" enter before "ventriloquism"?
options: If it occurs more frequently in the input text
Only if the vocabulary is bigram-only
questions.answer: If it occurs more frequently in the input text
questions.explanation: Terms are ranked by frequency regardless of n-gram order. Neither type has priority, and the bigram-only scheme wouldn't contain "ventriloquism" at all.

questions.question: A review has 200 tokens. How many unigrams and bigrams (with repeats) does TextVectorization(ngrams=2) generate before vocabulary lookup?
questions.answer: 200 unigrams + 199 bigrams = 399 terms.
questions.explanation: There are L - n + 1 n-grams per order. The multi-hot vector then records only which distinct terms are present in the vocabulary.

questions.question: Could you rewrite listing 14.12 into listing 14.16 from memory, naming each change and why it is needed?
questions.answer: max_tokens 20,000 -> 30,000 (room for bigrams); add ngrams=2 (generate bigrams); re-run adapt() (a new vocabulary that contains bigrams); rename the datasets bigram_*.
questions.explanation: Everything else (split, multi_hot, parallel map) stays the same, which is what makes the comparison with the unigram model fair.

questions.question: Why does x.shape equal (32, 30000) for a batch of bigram_train_ds?
questions.answer: 32 is the batch size, and 30,000 is max_tokens: the multi-hot vector has one position per vocabulary term (unigram or bigram).
questions.explanation: Listing 14.16 sets max_tokens = 30_000 with output_mode="multi_hot".

questions.question: Which entry in the vocabulary slice is a unigram?
questions.answer: "dont"
questions.explanation: "dont" is one token ("don't" with the apostrophe stripped); the other three are two-word bigrams.

questions.question: How many parameters does build_linear_classifier produce for max_tokens = 30,000, and how many more than the bag-of-words model?
questions.answer: 30,001 parameters; 10,000 more than the 20,001 of the unigram model.
questions.explanation: Dense(1) has one weight per input plus one bias: 30,000 + 1.

questions.question: What test accuracy does the bigram model reach?
questions.explanation: Listing 14.18 prints 0.90116. 0.88388 is the unigram model (p.426); the others are not on the page.

questions.question: Give the two reasons the book offers for why n-gram models beyond trigrams become impractical.
questions.answer: (1) The space of possible 4-grams is immense and grows exponentially with length, so decent coverage needs an immense vocabulary. (2) The model would lose its ability to generalize, memorizing entire snippets of sentences with weights attached.
questions.explanation: Both are stated in the last paragraph; together they motivate the more advanced sequence models.

questions.question: Why does the bigram model train in about the same time despite having 50% more parameters?
questions.answer: The model is tiny either way; training cost is dominated by tokenizing and encoding text on the CPU rather than by the parameter updates.
questions.explanation: p.425 noted that encoding is more expensive than updating the parameters, and the page says it trains in about the same amount of time.

questions.question: Can you explain why reusing build_linear_classifier unchanged makes the 88% -> 90% comparison meaningful?
questions.answer: Only the features changed (unigrams -> unigrams + bigrams); architecture, optimizer, loss, epochs and early stopping stayed the same, so the gain can be attributed to the bigram features.
questions.explanation: This is a controlled experiment that changes one variable at a time.

questions.question: Pad or truncate "the slow brown badger" and "the quick brown fox jumped over the lazy dog" to length 8.
questions.answer: [the, slow, brown, badger, [PAD], [PAD], [PAD], [PAD]] and [the, quick, brown, fox, jumped, over, the, lazy] ("dog" is dropped).
questions.explanation: Short sequences get [PAD] tokens at the end; long ones are cut after the 8th token, as shown in the page's example.

questions.question: Why must inputs be padded or truncated to a common length?
options: Because the vocabulary has a fixed size
So batches are rectangular and computation can be parallelized across the batch on a GPU
To make reviews have the same sentiment distribution
questions.answer: So batches are rectangular and computation can be parallelized across the batch on a GPU
questions.explanation: That is the reason given on the page. Vocabulary size limits which tokens exist, not sequence length; padding doesn't remove [UNK] tokens; and sentiment distribution is unrelated.

questions.question: Why do the authors move from n-gram features to sequence models?
questions.answer: n-gram features are manually engineered and only scale to a local ordering of a few words. Deep learning prefers to expose the model to the raw sequence and let it learn positional dependencies itself.
questions.explanation: Stated at the start of 14.5, building on the intractability argument of p.428.

questions.question: Which is NOT one of the sequence-model architectures listed on the page?
questions.answer: Multi-hot linear classifier
questions.explanation: The multi-hot linear classifier is the set model of section 14.4; the page lists RNNs, 1D ConvNets and Transformers.

questions.question: If a review has 233 tokens and sequences are padded to 600, how many [PAD] positions does it get, and what fraction of the sequence is padding?
questions.answer: 600 - 233 = 367 pad positions, about 61% of the sequence.
questions.explanation: Uses the average length of 233 quoted on the page. This much padding is why the book warns that pads must not affect predictions.

questions.question: Justify the choice of 600 as the truncation length for IMDb.
questions.answer: It keeps the input size manageable while losing little: the average review is 233 words and only 5% of reviews are longer than 600.
questions.explanation: Both statistics are given in the last paragraph.

questions.question: Can you explain the difference between [UNK] and [PAD], and why padding needs special care in a model?
questions.answer: [UNK] replaces a real word missing from the vocabulary; [PAD] is meaningless filler that equalizes lengths. Pads could distort predictions if the model treats them as content, so they need care (such as masking).
questions.explanation: Relates p.410 ([UNK]) to this page ([PAD]).

questions.question: Which TextVectorization argument in listing 14.19 pads and truncates sequences to 600 tokens?
questions.answer: output_sequence_length
questions.explanation: The callout "Pads and truncates to 600 tokens" points to output_sequence_length=max_length. max_tokens sets vocabulary size, split sets tokenization, and output_mode="int" sets the output type.

questions.question: What do the zeros at the end of each row of the printed batch represent?
questions.answer: Padding: index 0 is reserved for [PAD], filling positions after a review shorter than 600 tokens ends.
questions.explanation: The text: "almost all training samples have a number of 0s for padding at the end"; p.429 says the padding token is at index zero.

questions.question: How does listing 14.19 differ from listing 14.16, and why does that difference matter for sequence models?
questions.answer: It outputs integer token sequences (output_mode="int", fixed length 600) instead of a multi-hot vector with bigrams. The order of tokens is preserved, which is what a sequence model needs.
questions.explanation: Multi-hot discards order (set model); int sequences keep it.

questions.question: After one-hot encoding with max_tokens = 30,000, how many float values does one batch of shape (32, 600) contain?
questions.explanation: Each of the 19,200 token positions becomes a 30,000-dimensional vector, so the shape is (32, 600, 30000), confirmed on p.431.

questions.question: Why can't integer token IDs be fed directly as numeric inputs?
options: They are categorical labels whose numeric values carry no meaningful order or magnitude
Integers can't be stored on GPUs
questions.answer: They are categorical labels whose numeric values carry no meaningful order or magnitude
questions.explanation: The page says IDs must be mapped to floating-point data. IDs are indices, so treating them as magnitudes would be meaningless. The other options are false.

questions.question: How is one-hot encoding related to the multi-hot encoding used for the set models?
questions.answer: One-hot gives one vector per token, with a single 1; multi-hot gives one vector per whole review, with 1s for every token present (the combination of its tokens' one-hot vectors).
questions.explanation: The page calls one-hot "similar to the multi-hot encoding we did for an entire sequence".

questions.question: Looking at the printed batch, can you explain why the first IDs of each row differ widely in magnitude (e.g. 3 vs. 25819)?
questions.answer: The vocabulary is ordered by frequency, so small IDs are common words and large IDs rare ones. The magnitude says nothing about meaning, which is why one-hot (or embeddings) is needed.
questions.explanation: This connects vocabulary construction (adapt) to the need for categorical encoding.

questions.question: Why does gathering rows of ops.eye(depth) produce one-hot vectors?
questions.answer: Row i of the identity matrix has a 1 at position i and 0s elsewhere, which is exactly the one-hot vector of token i. ops.take with the token IDs selects the matching row for each token.
questions.explanation: These are the callouts "Builds an identity matrix with all possible one-hot vectors" and "Uses our input token IDs to gather the correct vector for each token".

questions.question: What is the output shape of one_hot_encoding(x) for a batch x of shape (32, 600) with max_tokens = 30,000?
questions.explanation: The final reshape restores the input shape and appends depth. (19200, 30000) is the intermediate shape before unflattening; (32, 30000) would be a multi-hot vector per review.

questions.question: Why is a bidirectional LSTM appropriate for classification but not for text generation?
questions.answer: In classification the whole review is available, so information can flow both forward and backward. In generation the future tokens don't exist yet, so each token's state may depend only on earlier tokens (a unidirectional model).
questions.explanation: Stated in the paragraph after the shape check.

questions.question: What does the line flat_inputs = ops.reshape(ops.cast(inputs, "int"), [-1]) do?
options: Casts the IDs to integers and flattens them into a 1-D vector
questions.answer: Casts the IDs to integers and flattens them into a 1-D vector
questions.explanation: Callout "Flattens the inputs". The identity matrix comes from ops.eye, padding happens in TextVectorization (p.430), and no normalization is done.

questions.question: How many parameters does the final Dense(1) layer have in listing 14.21, and why?
questions.answer: 129: 128 weights (one per feature of the concatenated bidirectional output) plus 1 bias.
questions.explanation: Bidirectional(LSTM(64)) concatenates two 64-dim states into 128; the summary on p.432 confirms 129.

questions.question: Why is the OneHotEncoding layer written with keras.ops rather than, say, NumPy or TensorFlow functions?
questions.answer: keras.ops is backend-agnostic, so the layer runs inside the model on JAX, TensorFlow or PyTorch (the chapter's outputs were produced with JAX, p.426).
questions.explanation: The listing title stresses "with Keras ops"; multi-backend support is emphasized in the sidebar on p.426.

questions.question: Can you trace the shapes of a (32, 600) batch through every line of OneHotEncoding.call and then through listing 14.21 to the output?
questions.explanation: If you can do this without looking, you understand both listings.

questions.question: Show how the Bidirectional layer gets 15,393,280 parameters, given hidden_dim = 64 and a one-hot depth of 30,000.
questions.explanation: An LSTM has four transforms (three gates plus the candidate), each with an input kernel (d×h), a recurrent kernel (h×h) and a bias (h). Bidirectional doubles the count.

questions.question: Why does the Dense layer have 129 parameters?
options: It has 128 inputs from the concatenated BiLSTM states plus 1 bias
It has 64 inputs times 2 outputs plus 1 bias
questions.answer: It has 128 inputs from the concatenated BiLSTM states plus 1 bias
questions.explanation: The Bidirectional output is (None, 128), and Dense(1) needs 128 weights plus one bias. The layer has a single output unit, not two or 129, and Dropout has no parameters.

questions.question: How many floating-point numbers represent a single review after one-hot encoding, and why?
questions.answer: 18,000,000, because the review is a matrix of 600 tokens × 30,000 vocabulary entries.
questions.explanation: The text states 600 words per sample and 30,000 possible words, so 600 × 30,000 = 18 million.
