questions.question: What test accuracy does the one-hot LSTM reach in Listing 14.23, and how does it compare?
questions.answer: 0.84811, worse than both set models
questions.explanation: Listing 14.23 prints 0.84811. 0.88388 and 0.90116 are the bag-of-words (p.426) and bigram (p.428) results, and no model in this chapter reaches 0.95.

questions.question: The model has about 500 times more parameters than the bigram model, yet performs worse. Give two reasons, based on this page and what follows.
questions.answer: (1) The one-hot input is extremely high-dimensional and sparse, so most of the computation and most of the parameters are wasted, and words share no information. (2) With only 20,000 training reviews, a 15M-parameter model cannot learn good per-word representations or order patterns before it overfits.
questions.explanation: This page blames the large inputs. Page 433 explains that one-hot vectors assume all words are unrelated, and pp.437 and 443 point to the data constraint.

questions.question: What does the early_stopping callback in Listing 14.22 do, and where is it defined?
questions.answer: It monitors val_loss, stops training if it does not improve for 2 epochs, and restores the best weights. It is defined on p.424.
questions.explanation: It is EarlyStopping(monitor="val_loss", restore_best_weights=True, patience=2), so epochs=10 is only an upper bound.

questions.question: Without looking, can you rebuild the summary table: each layer's output shape and parameter count?
questions.explanation: If you can derive each number, you understand the shapes in a one-hot recurrent pipeline.

questions.question: What assumption does one-hot encoding inject about words, according to the page?
options: That all tokens are independent of one another
That frequent words are more important
That word order does not matter
That synonyms share the same index
questions.answer: That all tokens are independent of one another
questions.explanation: The text says one-hot encoding assumes tokens are independent, since their vectors are orthogonal. It says nothing about frequency, and word order is a separate matter (set vs. sequence models). Synonyms get different indices.

questions.question: Compute the dot product and the L2 distance between the one-hot vectors of "movie" (index 1) and "film" (index 2) in a 4-word vocabulary.
questions.answer: Dot product 0; L2 distance √2 ≈ 1.414.
questions.explanation: [0,1,0,0]·[0,0,1,0] = 0, and the difference [0,1,-1,0] has norm √2. Any two distinct words give the same values, which is exactly the problem.

questions.question: List the three properties of one-hot vectors and the three of word embeddings shown in figure 14.3.
questions.answer: One-hot: sparse, high-dimensional, hardcoded. Embeddings: dense, lower-dimensional, learned from data.
questions.explanation: These are the labels and caption of figure 14.3.

questions.question: Why should a good embedding space make geometric distance relate to semantic distance? What does a model gain?
questions.answer: If similar words have similar vectors, whatever the model learns about one word automatically applies to its neighbors, so it generalizes from less data. With orthogonal vectors each word must be learned separately.
questions.explanation: This is the inference behind the authors' "movie"/"film" example. Linear layers respond similarly to similar inputs.

questions.question: Which embedding dimensionalities does the page call common for very large vocabularies?
questions.explanation: The text gives those numbers. 30,000 is the one-hot size for this vocabulary, 2D is only for toy plots (p.434), and vocabulary-sized vectors are one-hot.

questions.question: Name the two geometric distances the page offers as examples.
questions.answer: Cosine distance and L2 (Euclidean) distance.
questions.explanation: They are mentioned in the second paragraph of 14.5.2.

questions.question: Can you explain to a friend, in two sentences, why an Embedding layer should beat one-hot encoding for an LSTM?
questions.answer: Embeddings are small, dense and learned, so the model is faster and similar words can share what is learned. One-hot vectors are huge, sparse and treat every word as unrelated.
questions.explanation: Check yourself against the summary and figure 14.3.

questions.question: In figure 14.4, which pair of moves uses the same "from canine to feline" vector?
questions.answer: dog → cat and wolf → tiger
questions.explanation: The text says this vector moves dog → cat and wolf → tiger. cat → tiger and dog → wolf use the pet → wild vector. The other options mix relations or reverse directions.

questions.question: Using the approximate figure coordinates cat (0.72, 0.38), tiger (0.75, 0.80) and dog (0.40, 0.45), predict wolf's position by applying the pet → wild vector to dog.
questions.explanation: A shared displacement means wolf ≈ dog + (tiger − cat).

questions.question: What are the input and output shapes of the Embedding layer?
questions.answer: Input: an integer tensor (batch_size, sequence_length). Output: a float tensor (batch_size, sequence_length, embedding_size).
questions.explanation: This is stated in the last paragraph of the page.

questions.question: Give the authors' reasons why there is no single ideal word-embedding space.
questions.answer: None has been computed; there are many languages, which are not isomorphic because each reflects its own culture and context; and the useful semantic relationships differ by task (movie sentiment vs. legal classification).
questions.explanation: These are the three points of the first paragraph of 14.5.3.

questions.question: How does the book say the Embedding layer is best understood?
options: As a dictionary mapping integer indices to dense vectors
As a convolution over token sequences
As a fixed hash of each word
questions.answer: As a dictionary mapping integer indices to dense vectors
questions.explanation: The text calls it "effectively a dictionary lookup". It is not a convolution or a recurrence, and it is learned rather than a fixed hash.

questions.question: What is the "plural vector" example given on the page?
questions.answer: Adding a plural vector to "king" gives "kings".
questions.explanation: It is one of the two real-world examples, alongside king + female → queen.

questions.question: Can you explain why learning the embedding jointly with the task is "easy" in Keras, and what exactly is being learned?
questions.answer: The embedding table is just the Embedding layer's weights, trained by backpropagation like any other layer.
questions.explanation: Revisit the paragraph "It’s thus reasonable to learn a new embedding space..." and p.435.

questions.question: In Listing 14.24, what do input_dim and output_dim equal?
questions.answer: input_dim = 30,000 (max_tokens), output_dim = 64
questions.explanation: input_dim=max_tokens (30,000) and output_dim=hidden_dim (64). 600 is the sequence length, not the id range. 128 is the BiLSTM output size.

questions.question: How many parameters does the Embedding layer of Listing 14.24 have?
questions.explanation: One 64-dimensional vector per possible id; no bias.

questions.question: In figure 14.5, which integer does "arrow" map to, and what does the Embedding layer return for it?
questions.answer: 3; the vector stored in row 3 of the embedding table.
questions.explanation: "arrow" and 3 are highlighted in red, along with row 3 of the table.

questions.question: How are the Embedding layer's weights initialized, and how do they become meaningful?
questions.answer: Randomly, like any layer. Backpropagation adjusts them during training until the space has structure useful for the specific task.
questions.explanation: This is stated in the paragraph after figure 14.5.

questions.question: Which part of the model differs between Listing 14.21 and Listing 14.24?
questions.answer: Only the input encoding layer
questions.explanation: Both use hidden_dim = 64, binary cross-entropy and Dropout(0.5). Only OneHotEncoding is replaced by Embedding.

questions.question: Compute the parameter count of Bidirectional(LSTM(64)) when its input is the 64-dimensional embedding.
questions.explanation: Four gate transforms with input kernel, recurrent kernel and bias, in two directions.

questions.question: Can you sketch figure 14.5 from memory and label the tokenizer, ids and embedding table?
questions.answer: Tokens → Tokenizer → integer ids 0-7 → each id selects a row of the table.
questions.explanation: If you can, you understand what an Embedding layer computes.

questions.question: What does mask_zero=True do in the Embedding layer?
options: Marks positions whose token id is 0 so later layers can ignore them
Sets the embedding vector of id 0 to all zeros and keeps it fixed
Removes padded positions, shortening the sequence
Zeros out embeddings with small norm
questions.answer: Marks positions whose token id is 0 so later layers can ignore them
questions.explanation: Keras marks all elements whose input was 0 (the [PAD] id) and the LSTM uses the mask. The sequence length is unchanged, and nothing is zeroed or frozen.

questions.question: For ["the", "movie", "was", "awful", "[PAD]"×4], which token's representation do we want the LSTM to output?
questions.answer: "awful", the last non-padding token.
questions.explanation: This is stated explicitly on the page.

questions.question: Why does the summary contain a not_equal (NotEqual) layer with output (None, 600)?
questions.answer: It computes the mask ids != 0 created by mask_zero=True, and the Bidirectional layer takes it as a second input.
questions.explanation: The "Connected to" column shows bidirectional_1 receiving embedding[0][0] and not_equal[0][0].

questions.question: Verify the Bidirectional layer's 66,048 parameters.
questions.explanation: The input dimension is the embedding size of 64, and there are 64 units.

questions.question: How can you apply a custom mask, other than for id 0, to an LSTM?
options: Pass it via the LSTM's optional mask call argument
Set mask_zero to the id you want masked
Use Dropout with rate 1.0 on those steps
questions.answer: Pass it via the LSTM's optional mask call argument
questions.explanation: The page says the LSTM takes an optional mask call argument. mask_zero is a boolean only for id 0, and dropout is not masking.

questions.question: What inconsistency can you spot in the printed summary's "Connected to" column?
questions.answer: It references input_layer_6, bidirectional_2 and dropout_2, while the layers are named input_layer_3, bidirectional_1 and dropout_1.
questions.explanation: The output was apparently taken from different runs; it is cosmetic.

questions.question: Can you explain in your own words what an LSTM does at a masked timestep?
questions.answer: It skips the update and carries the previous hidden and cell states forward, so the final output is the state after the last real token.
questions.explanation: This is the mechanism behind "it will output the last non-masked representation".

questions.question: What test accuracy does Listing 14.25 report?
questions.explanation: That is the printed output. 0.84811 is the one-hot LSTM (p.432), 0.90116 the bigram model (p.428), and 99% is the training accuracy, not test accuracy.

questions.question: Why, according to the authors, did the embedding not improve accuracy?
questions.answer: The 20,000 training reviews are too few to learn a good word embedding. The model overfits (train accuracy above 99%) before it learns optimal embeddings.
questions.explanation: The authors blame the training setup (data), not the concept of embeddings.

questions.question: What does pretraining mean here, and what does it not require?
questions.answer: Training the word embedding separately, on more data, instead of jointly with the classifier. It does not require positive/negative review labels.
questions.explanation: This is stated in the last paragraph before the sidebar.

questions.question: By what factor did the parameter count shrink (15,393,409 → 1,986,177)? Is "an order of magnitude" accurate?
questions.answer: About 7.75×. That is roughly, but not quite, an order of magnitude (10×).

questions.question: Which improvement did the Embedding layer clearly bring?
options: Much smaller model and faster training
Higher test accuracy than the bigram model
questions.answer: Much smaller model and faster training
questions.explanation: The page says size and training time fell by an order of magnitude. Accuracy stayed at about 84% (below bigrams at 90%), the model still overfits, and padding is still used, now masked.

questions.question: According to the sidebar, how effective is text augmentation compared with image augmentation, and what is one basic technique?
questions.answer: It works but is not nearly as effective. Example: randomly deleting words (or swapping them, p.438).
questions.explanation: The sidebar begins on this page and continues on p.438.

questions.question: Could you explain to someone why a more efficient model is not automatically a more accurate one, using this page's experiment?
questions.answer: Efficiency comes from a better representation of the input; accuracy is limited by how much information the training data provides. Both LSTMs had to learn word representations from the same 20,000 reviews.
questions.explanation: Revisit the paragraphs "However..." and "Quite the contrary...".

questions.question: According to the sidebar, why has text augmentation not become widespread?
options: Edits easily change an example's meaning because language is order-dependent and sensitive to small changes
Augmented text makes models less robust to typos
Keras has no text augmentation layers
questions.answer: Edits easily change an example's meaning because language is order-dependent and sensitive to small changes
questions.explanation: The book names unintentional meaning changes as the big pitfall. Text is easy to edit, the book says augmentation can improve robustness to typos, and nothing is said about Keras layers.

questions.question: What two edits turn "The rain in Spain falls mainly on the plain" into "The rain Spain falls plain on the mainly"?
questions.answer: The word "in" is deleted, and "mainly" and "plain" are swapped.
questions.explanation: The sidebar lists random deletion (p.437) and swapping (p.438); the example shows both at once.

questions.question: Why is cropping a cat photo a safer augmentation than swapping two words in a review?
questions.answer: A cropped or rotated cat is still recognizably a cat, so the label is preserved; swapping words can change the meaning of a sentence, even to its opposite, so the label may no longer be correct.
questions.explanation: This is the contrast the book draws between image and text data.

questions.question: What makes pretraining possible without labeled data?
options: Using the test set as training data
An unsupervised task whose targets come from the text itself, such as guessing a missing word
Using one-hot encoding instead of embeddings
questions.answer: An unsupervised task whose targets come from the text itself, such as guessing a missing word
questions.explanation: The book: devise an unsupervised task to train parameters that do not need labeled data. Using the test set would be leakage, and the other two options are unrelated to pretraining.

questions.question: What is in the IMDb unsup/ directory, and why is it useful now when it was ignored before?
questions.answer: 25,000 unlabeled reviews. They were useless for supervised classification but can be used for the unsupervised CBOW task that pretrains the Embedding layer.
questions.explanation: The page reminds the reader of unsup/ and says all the text will be combined for pretraining.

questions.question: Connect this page to p.437: what problem does pretraining the embedding address?
questions.answer: With only 20,000 labeled reviews, the LSTM overfit (over 99% train accuracy) before learning good word embeddings and stalled near 84%. Pretraining learns the embeddings separately on more data without needing labels.
questions.explanation: The authors diagnose a data shortage, not a flaw of embeddings, and propose pretraining as the fix.

questions.question: Can you explain in your own words what CBOW predicts and what part of it we keep after training?
questions.answer: It predicts the middle word of a window from the surrounding words; we keep the learned embedding vectors.
questions.explanation: The page introduces CBOW; p.439 completes the description, and p.442 reuses only the embedding weights.

questions.question: In CBOW, what is the training target for each window?
options: The sentiment label of the review
The middle word of the window
The next word after the window
The first word of the review
questions.answer: The middle word of the window
questions.explanation: The middle word is the label and the other eight words are the context. Sentiment labels are not used in pretraining; predicting the next word is causal language modeling (chapter 15), not CBOW.

questions.question: Why does Listing 14.26 call text_vectorization.get_vocabulary() instead of adapting a new vocabulary?
questions.answer: So that every word gets the same token ID as in the LSTM classifier; then the pretrained embedding rows line up with the classifier's IDs and can be transferred.
questions.explanation: The page says the earlier vocabulary is reused and the goal is a 64-d vector for each word in this vocabulary.

questions.question: Why must the pretraining tokenizer not pad or truncate?
questions.answer: Truncation would discard text (and thus training windows), and padding would create meaningless windows made of padding tokens. Windows should be taken from the real token sequence.
questions.explanation: The page specifies a layer that does not truncate or pad before sliding a window over the text.

questions.question: With context_size = 4, how many tokens are in each window, and how many windows does a 50-token review yield?
questions.answer: 9 tokens per window; 50 - 8 = 42 windows.
questions.explanation: 2 x 4 + 1 = 9, and every position with four tokens on each side can be a middle word: n - 2 x context_size windows (the formula in window_data on p.440).

questions.question: What does figure 14.6 predict from "the", "quick", "fox", "jumped"?
questions.answer: "brown"
questions.explanation: The target word box in figure 14.6 is "brown", the word between "quick" and "fox". The other words come from the rest of the familiar sentence but are not the target shown.

questions.question: Does using tf.data for preprocessing mean the CBOW model must be trained with the TensorFlow backend?
questions.answer: No. The book says this choice does not limit the backend used for training.
questions.explanation: Keras 3 can feed a tf.data.Dataset into fit() on JAX, PyTorch or TensorFlow.

questions.question: Can you explain why predicting "boat" or "ocean" from "sail", "wave", "mast" would make those words' embeddings meaningful?
questions.answer: To predict well, words appearing in similar contexts must produce similar context vectors and outputs, so related words end up close together in the embedding space.
questions.explanation: This is the intuition behind CBOW described on pp.438-440.

questions.question: A tokenized review has 20 tokens. How many windows does window_data produce, and what is the shape of the index matrix?
questions.answer: 20 - 8 = 12 windows; the index matrix has shape (12, 9).
questions.explanation: num_windows = max(n - 2 x context_size, 0), and the matrix has one row per window and window_size = 9 columns.

questions.question: Why does this pipeline include the unsup/ reviews?
options: Because it reads the original imdb_extract_dir / "train" directory, which contains pos/, neg/ and unsup/
questions.answer: Because it reads the original imdb_extract_dir / "train" directory, which contains pos/, neg/ and unsup/
questions.explanation: The callout says "Uses all training data, including the unsup/ directory". The other functions only transform reviews that have already been loaded.

questions.question: What does dataset.map(lambda x, y: x) do, and why is it needed?
questions.answer: It drops the class label from each (text, label) pair. CBOW creates its own labels (the middle word), so the directory-based class (pos/neg/unsup) is not needed.
questions.explanation: Callout "Drops label".

questions.question: Why does averaging the context embeddings make CBOW a "bag of words" model?
questions.answer: The mean does not depend on the order of its inputs, so any permutation of the eight context words gives the same vector; only which words are present matters.
questions.explanation: GlobalAveragePooling1D computes the average of the bag.

questions.question: What is the output shape after layers.GlobalAveragePooling1D()(x) in Listing 14.28?
questions.answer: (None, 64)
questions.explanation: It averages over the 8 positions of (None, 8, 64). (None, 8) is the input, (None, 8, 64) the embedding output, and (None, max_tokens) the Dense output on p.441.

questions.question: What would go wrong in split_label if you changed context_size to 3 without editing anything else?
questions.answer: window_size is still hard-coded to 9 while num_windows becomes n - 6, so the last two windows would index past the end of the review (tf.gather raises an out-of-range error on CPU). Even ignoring that, left = window[:3] takes positions 0-2 and right = window[4:] takes positions 4-8, so the bag skips position 3 and includes position 4, which is exactly the label window[4]: the model would be asked to predict a token it is given as input.
questions.explanation: window_size and the label index are hard-coded; window_size = 2 * context_size + 1 and label = window[context_size] would generalize.

questions.question: Can you explain how tf.range(window_size)[None, :] + tf.range(num_windows)[:, None] produces all window positions?
questions.answer: Broadcasting adds every start position (column) to every offset 0..8 (row), giving a matrix whose row i is i, i+1, ..., i+8.
questions.explanation: This is broadcasting from chapter 2 applied to index arithmetic.

questions.question: Verify the Dense layer's parameter count in the summary.
questions.explanation: A Dense layer has input_dim x units weights plus one bias per unit; the input is the 64-d average and there are max_tokens = 30,000 units.

questions.question: Why does calling cache() make later CBOW epochs more than three times faster?
options: It moves the model to the GPU
It stores the preprocessed batches in memory so tokenization and windowing are not repeated
questions.answer: It stores the preprocessed batches in memory so tokenization and windowing are not repeated
questions.explanation: The book says training is bottlenecked on CPU preprocessing; caching removes that cost after epoch 1. cache() does not move anything to the GPU, change the vocabulary, or freeze weights.

questions.question: Why is sparse_categorical_crossentropy used instead of categorical_crossentropy?
questions.answer: The labels are integer token IDs (the middle word's index), not one-hot vectors of length 30,000.
questions.explanation: split_label (p.440) returns label = window[4], an integer.

questions.question: Why do the authors call 12% accuracy reasonable?
questions.answer: There are 30,000 possible words for each guess, so chance is about 0.003%; and several words often fit the same context, so even a perfect model could not be always right.
questions.explanation: The page cites the 30,000 choices; the ambiguity point follows from the "boat or ocean" example on p.439.

questions.question: Which statement about the CBOW model's size is correct?
options: The Embedding and Dense layers each hold about half of the 3.87 million parameters
Only the Dense layer is trainable
questions.answer: The Embedding and Dense layers each hold about half of the 3.87 million parameters
questions.explanation: 1,920,000 + 1,950,000 = 3,870,000. Pooling has 0 parameters, 15 million was the one-hot LSTM (p.437), and all parameters are trainable.

questions.question: Why can this model use a batch size of 1024 without memory problems?
questions.answer: The model is tiny (3.87M parameters, ~15 MB) and its activations per example are small, so even a large batch fits easily in memory.
questions.explanation: The book: because the model is so simple, a large batch size speeds up training without memory constraints.

questions.question: Could you diagnose whether your own training run is preprocessing-bound, and what would you do about it?
questions.answer: Check whether the GPU is idle or epochs speed up when data is precomputed; if so, cache or precompute preprocessed data (in memory or on disk), or parallelize preprocessing.
questions.explanation: This generalizes the page's advice on cache().

questions.question: What does Listing 14.31 do?
options: Shares the CBOW layer between both models
Copies the CBOW embedding values into the LSTM's embedding variable
questions.answer: Copies the CBOW embedding values into the LSTM's embedding variable
questions.explanation: assign overwrites the variable's values. It does not share the layer, freeze anything (no trainable=False), or average.

questions.question: Why does the book say 'roughly 2 million' embedding parameters?
questions.answer: max_tokens x hidden_dim = 30,000 x 64 = 1,920,000.
questions.explanation: One 64-d vector per vocabulary entry; matches the CBOW summary on p.441.

questions.question: Why is Listing 14.30 kept identical to Listing 14.24?
questions.answer: So the accuracy change can be attributed to the pretrained initialization alone.
questions.explanation: It is a controlled comparison: 0.84436 (p.437) vs 0.89139 with the same architecture and training recipe.

questions.question: What two things must match between cbow_embedding and lstm_embedding for the transfer to make sense?
questions.answer: The shape (30,000 x 64) and the vocabulary/token-ID mapping.
questions.explanation: Shape mismatch raises an error; a vocabulary mismatch would silently assign vectors to the wrong words. p.439 reuses the IMDb vocabulary for CBOW.

questions.question: Is the embedding trained during Listing 14.32?
options: Yes, it is fine-tuned with the rest of the model
questions.answer: Yes, it is fine-tuned with the rest of the model
questions.explanation: Nothing sets trainable=False; the book calls the CBOW weights an initializer. The other options have no basis in the code.

questions.question: Where does 0.89139 sit among the chapter's results?
questions.answer: Above both earlier LSTMs (~0.848 and ~0.844) and the unigram model (0.884), below the bigram model (0.901).
questions.explanation: See p.432, p.437, p.426, p.428 and the discussion on p.443.

questions.question: Could you rewrite Listing 14.31 with get_weights/set_weights and explain the difference from freezing?
questions.answer: lstm_embedding.set_weights(cbow_embedding.get_weights()); freezing would additionally set lstm_embedding.trainable = False.
questions.explanation: Both copy values; freezing is a separate decision about training.

questions.question: According to the authors, why does the pretrained LSTM not beat the bigram model?
options: The CBOW embedding was the wrong size
questions.answer: It is still data-constrained
questions.explanation: The book says the model is expressive enough but needs much more training on ordered data. LSTMs do model order; the embedding matched in size; nothing blames bidirectionality.

questions.question: Order the unigram, bigram and pretrained LSTM models by test accuracy.
questions.answer: Unigram 0.884 < pretrained LSTM 0.891 < bigram 0.901.
questions.explanation: From p.426, p.442, p.428; the page says slightly better than unigram, slightly worse than bigram.

questions.question: What does the book say is the 'most critical' advantage of the Transformer models of the next chapter?
questions.answer: They are often trained on large amounts of English text including all word-order information, letting them learn statistical grammatical patterns.
questions.explanation: Being slightly better at long dependencies is secondary in the authors' account.

questions.question: Which is NOT one of the three tokenization steps listed in the summary?
questions.answer: Embedding
questions.explanation: The steps are standardization, splitting and indexing. Embedding comes after tokenization, mapping IDs to vectors.

questions.question: When would you deploy a bigram set model over a sequence model?
questions.answer: When compute is limited and you can sacrifice some accuracy; set models are fast and small.
questions.explanation: The authors call them often the most cost-effective approach in that setting.

questions.question: Which tokenization type is usually most effective with an expressive model and enough data?
questions.answer: Subword tokenization.
questions.explanation: Stated in the third summary bullet; it balances vocabulary size and sequence length.

questions.question: Can you explain why CBOW pretraining improved the LSTM but did not give it knowledge of word order?
questions.answer: CBOW averages context embeddings, so it learns co-occurrence, not order; order must still be learned from labeled data.
questions.explanation: This is an inference consistent with the book's emphasis on 'ordered data'; see p.440 for the averaging.

questions.question: According to the summary, how are embedding weights trained?
options: With a special closed-form solution computed from co-occurrence counts
They are fixed random projections and never trained
Only by a separate unsupervised algorithm before the model is built
questions.answer: Normally, with gradient descent
questions.explanation: The page states 'Embeddings can be trained normally with gradient descent.' Co-occurrence factorization exists outside the book but is not what is described. Embeddings start random but are trained (p.435). Separate pretraining is optional; the first embedding LSTM (p.437) trained its embedding jointly.

questions.question: Why does the book call sequence models 'data-hungry', and what evidence from the chapter supports it?
questions.answer: They have many parameters and must learn order-dependent patterns. With only about 20,000 labeled reviews the LSTM reached 99% train accuracy but about 84% validation accuracy, overfitting before it learned good embeddings.
questions.explanation: See p.437 (overfitting numbers) and p.443 (the diagnosis that the LSTM is still data-constrained).

questions.question: What makes the CBOW task 'unsupervised', even though it has a target for every example?
questions.answer: The target, the middle token, is taken from the text itself, so no human labels are needed. Any unlabeled text can supply training pairs.
questions.explanation: This is what lets pretraining use the 25,000 unlabeled `unsup/` reviews (p.438, p.440). Today this is often called self-supervised learning.

questions.question: In Chapter 14, which parameters were transferred from the pretraining task to the downstream task?
options: The embedding weights learned by the CBOW model
questions.answer: The embedding weights learned by the CBOW model
questions.explanation: Listing 14.31 (p.442) copies the CBOW embedding into the LSTM's Embedding layer. The CBOW model has no LSTM and no sentiment Dense layer to transfer. The vocabulary is shared, but it is not a learned parameter.

questions.question: Why is an embedding lookup more efficient than feeding one-hot vectors to the model?
questions.answer: A one-hot vector is as long as the vocabulary and almost all zeros. Multiplying it by a weight matrix just selects one row, so an embedding performs that selection directly and outputs a short dense vector, saving computation and parameters downstream.
questions.explanation: The chapter measured about an order-of-magnitude reduction in training time and model size (p.437).

questions.question: Without looking back, list the full Chapter 14 summary: tokenization steps, tokenization types, the two families of models, embeddings, pretraining. Which item would you explain least confidently?
questions.answer: Standardization, splitting, indexing; character, word, subword; set models vs. sequence models; embeddings; pretraining.
questions.explanation: The first items are on p.443 and the last two on this page. Revisit the matching section for any you could not explain.
